claim: The World Trade Center leasehold was insured for about $3.55 billion per occurrence, and the figure is usually described as Larry Silverstein overpaying for coverage he did not need on a building an insurer valued at $1.5 billion. Both halves of that are wrong. Insuring the complex was a condition of the lease, not an option: the Second Circuit's account of the transaction records that Silverstein Properties, having leased the World Trade Center from the Port Authority, "was required to insure it," and procured a primary layer plus eleven excess layers totalling roughly $3.5 billion on a per-occurrence basis. The amount was set by his lenders, who raised their requirement as the deal progressed — $2.3 billion, then $3.2 billion, then $3.55 billion immediately before closing. Silverstein's broker, Willis of New York, placed that cover across some two dozen carriers. The $1.5 billion was never an insurer's valuation of the towers; it was the coverage the Port Authority had previously carried across its entire property portfolio, the World Trade Center included. The program was also unfinished. By September 11 only one carrier in it, Allianz, had issued a final policy; every other insurer was still on a binder, which is why the coverage terms had to be litigated at all. The coverage tracked the price of the asset: the 99-year net lease was worth about $3.2 billion. Silverstein was not the sole leaseholder — he led a consortium including GMAC Commercial Mortgage and Westfield America — and the lease left him owing the Port Authority roughly $10 million a month in ground rent and obliged to rebuild. The two-occurrence litigation that followed, and the approximately $4.55 billion settlement reached in 2007, are documented separately.

notes: Backstage. Upgraded 2026-08-22 off the litigation record rather than press. Alison Frankel's "Double Indemnity" (The American Lawyer, September 3, 2002) is the origin of the lender-minimum fact and remains behind a paywall, but the Second Circuit's own account of the transaction turned out to be the stronger citation and says the thing that matters more plainly: Silverstein "was required to insure" the complex. That reframes the whole over-insured story — the argument is about the size of a mandatory policy, not about a man volunteering to buy cover. The binders detail is new here and is the most useful fact recovered: on September 11 the program was still unfinished, with only Allianz on a final policy and everyone else on binders whose occurrence definitions differed. A scheme premised on collecting a defined limit does not leave the limit undefined, and the entire multi-year litigation exists because it was. That cuts against the foreknowledge reading and the record states it without saying so. Group A on the correction; the foreknowledge inference the claim builds toward is Group B.
